15.0.s.en: (1) Abijam the son of Rehoboam, king over Judah

15.0.0.en: Abijam: He is also called Abijah (2 Chr 13:1). The reign of Jeroboam king of Israel was twenty-two years (ch. 14:20). Abijam ascended the throne of Judah in the eighteenth year of the reign of Jeroboam, and he continued to reign only three years. That is, Abijam king of Judah and Jeroboam king of Israel reigned at the same time for three years, and after the three years the reign of Jeroboam extended another year, during which he was a contemporary of Abijam's successor, Asa king of Judah.

15.1.0.en: The capital of his kingdom was Jerusalem, in which he reigned three years. His mother was Maachah, the granddaughter of Absalom the son of David (a granddaughter is often called a daughter), and Absalom was the son of David who led a revolt and drove his father out of the kingdom, so he was wicked, and his granddaughter Maachah was wicked like him. Abijam was not the firstborn of Rehoboam, but the son of Maachah, whom Rehoboam loved, and who is also called Michaiah in (2 Chr 13:2). Because she was strong in personality, she influenced the kingdom and set her son Abijam on the throne as king.

15.2.0.en: This verse describes very briefly the summary of what characterized the reign of Abijam: he followed the steps of his father Rehoboam, and his heart was not with God as was the heart of David his forefather, but he fell into the worship of idols and all the evils connected with it. This shows the influence of wicked fathers upon their children.

15.3.0.en: It is an Eastern custom to keep a lamp burning continually in the house, never put out unless the master of the house dies and the house is abandoned. Here God shows how He gave a lamp to David: although Rehoboam and his son Abijam were wicked, God gave Abijam a righteous son, Asa. God's honoring of the righteous David by giving him Asa, his righteous descendant, shows the standing of the saints with God even after their death. God preserved the kingship for David over the kingdom of Judah for 400 years, and after that He permitted the Babylonian captivity as discipline for them, but from his offspring came Christ, who reigns forever.

15.3.1.en: The reason for God's honoring David was his uprightness in the worship of God and his keeping away from evils, except on a few occasions, the most important of which was his fall into the sin of adultery with the wife of Uriah the Hittite and then the killing of her husband. But he repented quickly, for he did not persist in his sins and he loved God with all his heart. The mention of his sin here shows the mercies of God, and that every man is exposed to error, but if he repents God lifts his sin from him. God calls us to be careful: if the saints were exposed to falling, how much more the ordinary man! But the important thing is to hold fast to God, as David held fast to Him and rejected the worship of idols.

15.3.2.en: God opens the door of hope before you, however great your sins, so that you may return to Him quickly, obtain His mercies, regain your life with Him in holy worship and enjoy fellowship with Him.

15.4.0.en: This verse returns to confirm the bad relations between the two parts of the kingdom, Judah and Israel, for disputes and wars between them began from the time of Rehoboam and Jeroboam, as was mentioned earlier in (ch. 14:30), and the details of these wars are found in (2 Chr 13).

15.5.0.en: The wars between the kingdoms of Israel and Judah continued not only in the days of Rehoboam but also in the days of his son Abijam (ch. 14:30), but when Abijam took refuge in God, He gave him strength, so he triumphed over Jeroboam and called his people to return to God, as is mentioned in (2 Chr 13), and Jeroboam did not return to fight Abijam after Abijam's victory over him. The rest of the life of Abijam is recorded in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah, which is a book in which the records of the kings were written, other than the book of Chronicles that is in the Holy Bible.

15.6.0.en: The reign of Abijam was very short, three years, after which he died and was buried with his fathers in the city of David, and his son Asa reigned in his place.

15.7.0.en: After the death of Abijam, his son Asa reigned in his place over the kingdom of Judah, and this was in the twentieth year of the reign of Jeroboam, or the twentieth year of the division of the kingdom. We notice that Abijam reigned three years, from the eighteenth year to the twentieth of the reign of Jeroboam, because part of a year is counted as a year, which means that Abijam reigned less than three years.

15.7.1.en: God kept the kingship for the offspring of David despite the evil of Rehoboam and his son Abijam, and then came the righteous Asa. In Israel, however, the kingship changed among nine families over two and a half centuries, because all of them fell into evil.

15.8.0.en: The reign of Asa in Jerusalem was long, for he reigned 41 years, and this was a grace from God because he was righteous, so he was able to carry out many reforms during his long reign, a period longer than the reign of David and Solomon. The name of his grandmother, his father's mother, was Maachah the daughter of Absalom, and as we mentioned in (v. 2), a grandmother is sometimes called the mother, the meaning being the grandmother, and she is mentioned here because her personality was The First Book of Kings strong and dominated Rehoboam her husband and Abijam her son by her evil; but Asa did not submit to her, rather he removed her, as will appear in (v. 13).

15.9.0.en: The sodomites: those who practice sexual perversion as the passive partner.

15.9.1.en: The righteousness of Asa appeared in his cleansing his land of the worship of idols, for he removed all the idol worship that his father Abijam and his forefather Rehoboam had made. He also removed all the sins connected with these forms of worship, such as fornication and sexual perversion, so Asa removed the houses set apart for the practice of these sins, which were established beside the temples of the idols. But he was not able to remove all the houses of the sodomites, as is proved by the existence of some of them in the days of his son Jehoshaphat (ch. 22:46); but at least he was much better than his father and his forefather.

15.10.0.en: An idol in a grove: the grove was a pillar of wood or stone with a statue at its top of the goddess Ashtoreth, the goddess of the Sidonians.

15.10.1.en: The brook Kidron: a valley lying east of the city of Jerusalem, between it and the Mount of Olives, in which there was worship of pagan gods.

15.10.2.en: Asa was concerned to remove everything that encouraged the worship of idols. Despite the strength of his grandmother Maachah, who encouraged the worship of idols and had set up an idol in a grove for the worship of the goddess Ashtoreth, Asa deposed her, so that she dwelt in a private dwelling far from the palace, in order to nullify her authority and influence. Then he destroyed the wooden idol of the grove, burned it with fire and scattered its ashes in the valley of Kidron, where the pagan gods were worshiped, as a disdain and defilement of this worship.

15.11.0.en: Asa walked in the worship of God alone and removed the idols from Jerusalem and the places near it, but he did not remove all the high places around Jerusalem, which had begun in the days of Solomon (2 Chr 14:3). On these high places, in his days, the worship of God was offered, although this was an error against the Law, which commanded that worship be offered in the temple of God alone (Deut 12:11), in addition to the fact that in the days of Rehoboam and Abijam they offered worship to idols on the high places. This shows that Asa was righteous in removing the worship of idols, but not completely.

15.12.0.en: Abijam had triumphed over Jeroboam king of Israel and taken from him much spoil, which he sanctified to the Lord, and he placed in the treasuries of the house of the Lord quantities of gold and silver and the vessels made of them. Likewise his son Asa triumphed over Zerah the Ethiopian (2 Chr 14:9-15) and sanctified, that is, set apart, his spoils of war of gold and silver and placed them in the treasuries of the house of the Lord. This shows his love for the house of the Lord and not for his personal luxury.

15.13.0.en: Baasha rose up and killed Nadab the son of Jeroboam and all the offspring of Jeroboam, and reigned over Israel, and there were many wars between him and Asa for most of the days of Asa. The land had rest for only ten years (2 Chr 14:1).

15.14.0.en: Ramah: a small village built on a high plateau near the border of the tribe of Benjamin, ten kilometers north of Jerusalem on the road to Bethel.

15.14.1.en: Baasha began his preparations to fight the kingdom of Judah by building a village called Ramah very close to Jerusalem, for the following reasons:

15.14.2.en: 1- To make it easy to attack Jerusalem.

15.14.3.en: 2- Ramah was on a main road from Bethel to Jerusalem, and he wanted to prevent any trade with Jerusalem.

15.14.5.en: 3- To prevent the inhabitants of Israel from going to pray and keep the feasts in Jerusalem, lest they be influenced and follow King Asa.

15.14.6.en: 4- To prevent the emigration of those of the inhabitants of Israel who wished to live near Jerusalem.

15.15.0.en: Ben-hadad: He is Ben-hadad the First, the grandson of Hezion, who may be the same as Rezon who seized Damascus and opposed Solomon (ch. 11:23, 25). There is more than one king of Syria by this name: the second Ben-hadad was in the days of Ahab king of Israel, and the third was in the days of Jehoahaz king of Judah (ch. 20:1-34, 2 Kgs 13:3-13). Syria: present-day Syria.

15.15.1.en: This was one of the errors of Asa, for he did not turn to the Lord but to Ben-hadad king of Damascus to help him against Baasha. He gathered the gold and silver that were in the treasuries of the house of the Lord and the treasuries of his palace and gave them to the men with whom he sent a message to Ben-hadad. The quantities of gold and silver remaining in the treasuries were small, and they were what Abijam and Asa had gathered as spoil in their wars, because Shishak king of Egypt had taken the gold and silver from the treasuries before that (ch. 14:26). By this Asa gave the sacred things of God to the pagans, and that angered God.

15.16.0.en: In his message Asa reminded him of the alliance existing between them as it had existed between their fathers, and he presented him with gifts of silver and gold, asking him to break his covenant with Baasha king of Israel so that the latter would withdraw from fighting him. This, of course, was an error on the part of Asa. For instead of praying and relying on God, he asked Ben-hadad, a mighty king neighboring the two kingdoms, to support him, and he sent him gifts. Hanani the seer rebuked Asa for this conduct (2 Chr 16:7-10).

15.16.1.en: Whatever the threats or difficult circumstances you meet, do not take refuge in the world and its powers, but in God, for He alone is your helper, and let not your heart be troubled, because God who is with you is stronger than all. Pray first, and God will guide you to what you can use of the material things around you.

15.17.0.en: Ijon: a city in the northern part of the land of the children of Israel.

15.17.1.en: Abel-beth-maachah: a fortified city in Naphtali.

15.17.2.en: Cinneroth: a fortified city in Naphtali, known as the plain of Gennesaret (Mt 14:34). Ben-hadad heeded the call of King Asa and commanded his armies, and they attacked the cities of Israel and destroyed the cities of Ijon, Dan and Abel-beth-maachah and all the region of Cinneroth and all the land of Naphtali.

15.18.0.en: When Ben-hadad attacked the kingdom of Israel and seized some of its cities, Baasha was afraid and stopped building the city of Ramah, because he felt that Ben-hadad had broken the covenant with him and allied himself with Asa, and he feared that Ben-hadad would continue to overrun the cities of Israel. He could not fight two adversaries at the same time, Syria and Judah, so he withdrew and dwelt in his capital Tirzah.

15.19.0.en: None was exempted: he exempted no one from coming and taking part in the building.

15.19.1.en: Geba of Benjamin: a city in Benjamin on the northern edge of the kingdom of Judah. Today there is a village of the same name 6.5 km northeast of Jerusalem and close to Ramah.

15.19.2.en: Mizpah: a city in Benjamin that Asa fortified. The prophet Samuel used to live in it (1 Sam 7:16, 17). It is near Ramah, about 1.5 km away, and about 13 km from Jerusalem.

15.19.3.en: The First Book of Kings King Asa summoned all the men of the people and exempted no one from coming, to gather what Baasha had left of the stones and timber that he had intended to use in building Ramah, and King Asa used them to build the two cities "Geba of Benjamin and Mizpah."

15.20.0.en: The writer of the book teaches us that there are other details of the reign of Asa recorded in "the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah," and he also tells us that Asa was afflicted with a disease in his feet in the time of his old age. Details about the life of Asa are found in (2 Chr 14, 15, 16).

15.21.0.en: Asa died and was buried with his fathers in the city of David, and his son Jehoshaphat succeeded him on the throne of Judah.

15.22.s.en: (3) Nadab and Baasha reign over Israel

15.22.0.en: In the second year of Asa king of Judah, Nadab the son of Jeroboam began to reign over Israel, and his reign was very short, for he reigned only two years, which in reality is less than two years, that is, one year and some months, because he began to reign in the second year of Asa and Baasha succeeded him in the third year of Asa.

15.23.0.en: Nadab walked in the way of his father Jeroboam, in the worship of the two golden calves, and he prevented the people from going to Jerusalem and worshiping in the temple of the Lord.

15.24.0.en: Gibbethon: the name of a town in the portion of Dan. It lies directly east of Ekron, near the Mediterranean Sea, in the south of the land of the children of Israel.

15.24.1.en: Nadab was besieging Gibbethon, trying to recover it from the Philistines, because the Philistines had taken it from the children of Israel, and Baasha plotted against him and killed him there.

15.25.0.en: Nadab was killed in the third year of Asa king of Judah, and Baasha reigned in his place. Here begins the series of assassinations in the kingdom of Israel, which occurred nine times, and all of them were wicked and tried to seize the kingship from one another.

15.25.1.en: V. 29: The first thing Baasha did when he took the kingship was to kill all the offspring of Jeroboam and destroy his house completely, so the prophecy that Ahijah the Shilonite prophesied was fulfilled (ch. 14:10, 11). The First Book of Kings

15.26.0.en: That was a punishment for the sins of Jeroboam and for his driving his people into the same errors, when they worshiped pagan gods, forsaking the Lord their true God; by that they brought the wrath of the Lord upon themselves.

15.27.0.en: The writer of the book mentions that there is a civil history of the period of Nadab's reign written in "the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel," in which other details about the life of Nadab are mentioned.

15.28.0.en: As we saw in the preceding verses, there were wars between Asa king of Judah and Baasha king of Israel throughout the days of their reign; the era of peace had ended in the wake of Solomon's reign, and there were many wars between the kings of Judah and the kings of Israel, because of the two peoples' departure from God. The war meant is not only a great war, for the great war was in the sixteenth year of the reign of Asa, and the rest of the time there were skirmishes, and of course these wars weakened the kingdoms of Israel and Judah, which helped the surrounding nations to prevail over them. Perhaps the kingdom of Israel, despite its large size, felt its weakness because the temple of God was not in it, and therefore it feared the small kingdom of Judah and tried to attack it from time to time.

15.28.1.en: God was long-suffering with Jeroboam, but in the end the divine punishment had to be carried out by the destruction of his offspring who persisted in evil. Do not despise the long-suffering of God, but turn back from your sin, for He is merciful and ready to forgive it, however great or repeated it may be, and learn from the errors of others so as to keep away from them, and you will live in assurance.

15.29.0.en: In the third year of the reign of Asa king of Judah, Baasha the son of Ahijah began to reign over the kingdom of Israel, and the capital of his kingdom was "Tirzah," and he remained king for 24 years.

15.30.0.en: Baasha walked in the way of evil as Jeroboam walked, and he did not depart from the sin of the worship of idols which Jeroboam had devised, but he led his people Israel after him in the same crooked way. The kings of Israel from Baasha to Ahab
